headings.title: Introduction to Occupational Health Hazards
headings.content: Occupational health hazards are elements within the working environment that can cause physical or mental harm to workers. In Nigeria, workplaces ranging from informal mechanic workshops in Lagos to large multinational oil platforms in the Niger Delta present diverse risk profiles. Understanding these exposures allows nursing professionals to protect workers, prevent chronic illnesses, and promote safe labour practices. Occupational hazards are systematically categorized based on their nature into physical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, psychosocial, and mechanical factors.

headings.title: Physical Hazards in the Workplace
headings.content:
Physical hazards are environmental factors within the workplace that can harm the body without necessarily touching it directly. Common examples include extreme temperatures, noise, vibration, and ionizing or non-ionizing radiation.

- **Noise**: Excessive sound levels in textile mills or construction sites can cause permanent noise-induced hearing loss.
- **Vibration**: Hand-arm vibration from heavy power tools leads to conditions like hand-arm vibration syndrome or 'white finger'.
- **Radiation**: Welders face risks from ultraviolet radiation, while radiographers deal with ionizing X-rays.
- **Temperature extremes**: Heat stress is a major concern for outdoor agricultural workers and miners exposed to tropical Nigerian climates.

headings.title: Chemical Hazards and Toxic Exposures
headings.content: Chemical hazards manifest in various forms, including liquids, gases, vapours, fumes, and dusts. Workers can absorb these substances through inhalation, ingestion, or dermal contact. Acute exposure may trigger sudden chemical pneumonitis or systemic poisoning, whereas chronic exposure often results in organ damage or carcinogenesis. In industrial settings, volatile solvents and heavy metals like lead pose serious health threats. Proper ventilation, use of chemical-resistant gloves, and adherence to material safety data sheets are foundational defenses.

headings.title: Biological Hazards and Infectious Agents
headings.content:
Biological hazards involve living organisms that pose a threat to human health. Healthcare workers, laboratory technicians, veterinarians, and agricultural laborers face constant exposure to bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites, and bodily fluids. 

In clinical facilities across Nigeria, accidental needle-stick injuries put personnel at risk of contracting blood-borne pathogens such as Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Adhering to universal precautions, utilizing safety-engineered syringes, and ensuring up-to-date immunizations remain critical nursing interventions.

headings.title: Ergonomic Hazards and Musculoskeletal Risks
headings.content: Ergonomic hazards arise when job demands do not match the physical capabilities of the worker. Poor workstation design, repetitive motions, forceful exertions, and awkward postures place excessive strain on muscles, joints, and ligaments. Nursing itself is physically demanding; transferring heavy patients, bending over low hospital beds, and standing for prolonged shifts frequently lead to chronic lower back pain. Employers mitigate these risks by providing adjustable furniture, mechanical lifting aids, and training staff on proper body mechanics.

headings.title: Psychosocial Hazards and Workplace Stress
headings.content: Psychosocial hazards relate to the design, organization, and management of work, as well as its economic and social contexts. Factors such as high workload demands, role ambiguity, low job control, lack of social support, workplace violence, and bullying contribute heavily to chronic stress, burnout, and depression. In healthcare, understaffed wards and traumatic patient outcomes exacerbate mental exhaustion. Addressing psychosocial risks requires improving organizational communication, establishing mental health support programs, and promoting a healthy work-life balance.

headings.title: Mechanical and Safety Hazards
headings.content: Mechanical hazards involve unguarded machinery, moving parts, sharp edges, and pinch points that can cause cuts, crush injuries, amputations, or entrapment. Safety hazards encompass broader environmental trip and fall conditions, electrical faults, and fire risks. In poorly regulated industrial or construction environments, missing machine guards and faulty electrical wiring frequently cause catastrophic injuries. Regular safety audits, maintenance of equipment, and clear lockout-tagout protocols are vital preventive measures.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Hazard Identification
headings.content: Occupational health nursing involves proactive hazard identification, workplace risk assessment, and clinical intervention. Nurses conduct walkthrough surveys, review injury logs, and interview workers to uncover hidden hazards. By recognizing early signs of occupational diseases, nurses facilitate prompt treatment and rehabilitation. Education remains a cornerstone; teaching employees proper use of personal protective equipment and safe working habits transforms the workplace safety culture from reactive to preventative.
